title: Can you override `private` and `static` methods in Java (method hiding vs overriding)?
shortTitle: Can you override private and static methods?

s1_definition.profdef: You cannot override private or static methods in the true polymorphic sense. Private methods are not inherited and are not visible to subclasses, so a same-named method in a subclass is a brand-new unrelated method, not an override. Static methods belong to the class rather than to any instance, so a same-signature static method in a subclass hides the parent's static method rather than overriding it, and which one runs is decided at compile time by the reference type, not at runtime by the object type. True overriding, with runtime dynamic dispatch, applies only to non-static, non-private, non-final instance methods.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, overriding is like a specialist branch replacing the head-office procedure with its own, so that whenever a customer is served, the branch's version automatically runs based on who is actually serving. A private method is like an internal note locked in the head-office drawer that branches cannot even see, so a branch writing its own note with the same title is just its own private note, not a replacement. A static method is like a rule pinned to the whole organisation under a label; if a branch pins a different rule under the same label, which rule applies depends on which label you read from, the head office's or the branch's, decided up front, not by who is serving.
s1_definition.oneliner: Private methods are not inherited so cannot be overridden, static methods are hidden not overridden and resolved by reference type at compile time, and true runtime overriding applies only to instance methods.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** You cannot override private or static methods in the true polymorphic sense. Private methods are not inherited and are not visible to subclasses, so a same-named method in a subclass is a brand-new unrelated method, not an override. Static methods belong to the class rather than to any instance, so a same-signature static method in a subclass hides the parent's static method rather than overriding it, and which one runs is decided at compile time by the reference type, not at runtime by the object type. True overriding, with runtime dynamic dispatch, applies only to non-static, non-private, non-final instance methods.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, overriding is like a specialist branch replacing the head-office procedure with its own, so that whenever a customer is served, the branch's version automatically runs based on who is actually serving. A private method is like an internal note locked in the head-office drawer that branches cannot even see, so a branch writing its own note with the same title is just its own private note, not a replacement. A static method is like a rule pinned to the whole organisation under a label; if a branch pins a different rule under the same label, which rule applies depends on which label you read from, the head office's or the branch's, decided up front, not by who is serving.

**One line to remember:** Private methods are not inherited so cannot be overridden, static methods are hidden not overridden and resolved by reference type at compile time, and true runtime overriding applies only to instance methods.

sections.s2_technical:
Overriding means a subclass provides a new implementation for an inherited instance method, and at runtime the JVM dispatches to the actual object's version regardless of the reference type. This is dynamic dispatch and it is the heart of polymorphism.

Private methods break the first requirement: they are not inherited. A private method is invisible outside its own class, so a subclass cannot see it and cannot override it. If the subclass declares a method with the same name, it is simply a separate method that happens to share a name, with no overriding relationship, and the parent's private method still calls itself internally.

```java
class Account { private String tag() { return "ACCOUNT"; } String show() { return tag(); } }
class Savings extends Account { private String tag() { return "SAVINGS"; } } // NOT an override
// new Savings().show() still returns "ACCOUNT" — parent's private tag() is bound within Account
```

Static methods break the dispatch requirement differently. A static method with the same signature in a subclass does not override; it hides the parent's static method. Because static calls are resolved by the compiler using the reference type, the version chosen depends on the declared type, not the runtime object:

```java
class Account { static String type() { return "ACCOUNT"; } }
class Savings extends Account { static String type() { return "SAVINGS"; } } // hides, not overrides
Account ref = new Savings();
ref.type();        // "ACCOUNT" — resolved by reference type at compile time
Savings.type();    // "SAVINGS"
```

This is the key contrast: with instance methods, Account ref pointing to a Savings would run the Savings version through dynamic dispatch, but with static methods it runs the Account version because resolution is static.

A senior point is that you should never call a static method through an instance reference, because it looks like a virtual call but is not, which misleads readers; always call static methods through the class name to make the hiding explicit. Another senior point is that final and private instance methods are also non-overridable, final by rule and private by invisibility, and understanding this prevents the classic trap of expecting a subclass's static or private method to participate in polymorphism when it does not.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — A subclass defined a private method with the same name as the parent's, and a developer expected it to change the parent's behavior, but it did not. This is exactly why private methods cannot be overridden.

Problem 2 — A subclass defined a static method with the same signature, and which one ran depended on the reference type rather than the object. This is exactly static method hiding.

Problem 3 — A proper instance method override did change behavior through dynamic dispatch, providing the contrast. This is exactly true overriding.

The code defines an `Account` and a `Savings` subclass demonstrating a private non-override, a static hide, and a real instance override, driven by an `OverrideHidingDemo` main class.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is a single Savings object, referenced both directly as Savings and through an Account-typed reference pointing to the same object.

Step 1: Calling showTag on the Savings object runs the parent's showTag, which internally calls tag. Because tag is private, it is bound to Account's own tag within Account, so the result is the account tag, not the savings tag, proving the subclass's private method is not an override.

Step 2: Calling type through the Account class name returns the account type, and calling type through the Savings class name returns the savings type, which shows two independent static methods.

Step 3: Calling type through the Account-typed reference returns the account type, because static calls are resolved by the compiler using the reference type, not the runtime object, which is static method hiding in action.

Step 4: Calling label through the same Account-typed reference returns the savings label, because label is a true instance override and the JVM dispatches to the actual object's version at runtime.

Step 5: The contrast is explicit: for the static method the reference type won, while for the instance method the object type won, which is precisely the difference between hiding and overriding.

```
Oct 30, 2026 ... INFO: showTag() via Savings → ACCOUNT-tag
Oct 30, 2026 ... WARNING: Account.type() → ACCOUNT-type
Oct 30, 2026 ... WARNING: Savings.type() → SAVINGS-type
Oct 30, 2026 ... WARNING: ref.type() (ref is Account-typed) → ACCOUNT-type
Oct 30, 2026 ... INFO: ref.label() (true override) → SAVINGS-label
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  one object: new Savings(), referenced as Account ref

  PRIVATE (not inherited)
    savings.showTag() → Account.showTag() → Account.tag() → "ACCOUNT-tag"

  STATIC (hiding, compile-time by reference type)
    Account.type()   → "ACCOUNT-type"
    Savings.type()   → "SAVINGS-type"
    ref.type()       → "ACCOUNT-type"   (ref declared as Account)

  INSTANCE (overriding, runtime by object type)
    ref.label()      → "SAVINGS-label"  (dynamic dispatch to Savings)
```
sections.s5c_hld:
```
  ═══ HLD — Resolution Rules in a Service Hierarchy ═══

  ┌────────┐  REST  ┌──────────────────┐
  │ Client │───────→│ Account Service   │
  └────────┘        └───────┬──────────┘
                            │ instance method → runtime (object type)
                            │ static method   → compile-time (ref type)
                            │ private method  → invisible to subclass
                            ▼
                   polymorphism applies ONLY to instance methods
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Override vs Hide vs Hidden-by-Privacy ═══

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ───────────────────────────────┐
  │  L: Savings substitutes Account only via INSTANCE override│
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ──────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌───────────────────────────────┐
  │           Account             │
  │  - tag(): String              │ private (NOT inherited)
  │  + type(): String   [static]  │ hideable
  │  + label(): String            │ overridable
  └───────────────┬───────────────┘
                  │ extends
                  ▼
  ┌───────────────────────────────┐
  │           Savings             │
  │  - tag(): String              │ NEW private (not an override)
  │  + type(): String   [static]  │ HIDES Account.type()
  │  + label(): String  @Override │ OVERRIDES Account.label()
  └───────────────────────────────┘

  Resolution (in sentences):
    private → each class binds its own; no polymorphism
    static  → reference type decides at compile time (hiding)
    instance→ object type decides at runtime (overriding)

  ── Call Chain (Main Scenario) ─────────────────────────────

  1. savings.showTag() → ACCOUNT-tag  (private not overridden)
  2. ref.type()        → ACCOUNT-type (static hidden, ref type)
  3. ref.label()       → SAVINGS-label(instance overridden, object type)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
No, you cannot override private or static methods in the true polymorphic sense, and the reasons are different for each. Overriding means a subclass replaces an inherited instance method and the JVM dispatches to the actual object's version at runtime, which is dynamic dispatch and the core of polymorphism. Private and static methods each fail one of the conditions for that.

Private methods are not inherited. A private method is invisible outside its own class, so a subclass cannot see it and cannot override it. If the subclass declares a method with the same name, it is just a separate, unrelated method, and the parent's own code still calls the parent's private version. I showed this with a parent showTag that calls a private tag, where the subclass's same-named private tag had no effect and the parent tag still ran.

Static methods belong to the class, not to any instance, so a same-signature static method in a subclass hides the parent's static method rather than overriding it. The crucial consequence is that static calls are resolved by the compiler using the reference type, not the runtime object, so an Account-typed reference pointing to a Savings object runs the Account static method. I contrast this directly with an instance method, where the same Account-typed reference runs the Savings version through dynamic dispatch. That side-by-side is the clearest way to state the difference: for static methods the reference type wins at compile time, for instance methods the object type wins at runtime.

The senior habits that follow are to never call a static method through an instance reference, because it looks like a virtual call but is not and misleads readers, and to always call static methods through the class name so the hiding is explicit. I also remember that final and private instance methods are non-overridable too, final by rule and private by invisibility. So my complete answer is that private methods cannot be overridden because they are not inherited, static methods are hidden and resolved by reference type at compile time, and true runtime overriding applies only to non-static, non-private, non-final instance methods.

---

keyPoints: private methods: not inherited, cannot be overridden
static methods: hidden, not overridden — resolved by reference type
Hiding: child defines same-signature static method, hides parent version
@Override on a static method causes compile error
